newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim reopens debate on loathed labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim reopens debate on loathed labour law.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam agreed on Tuesday to reopen parliamentary debate on a controversial new labour law in a stunning concession to opposition parties following more than three weeks of strikes.
During a meeting with heads of three main political parties he also climbed down on another controversial bill reviving the powers of the once notorious domestic spy agency.
"Anything can be discussed in parliament again, whether it is the labour law or the law on the Agency for National Security Planning," a presidential spokesman quoted Kim as saying.
Kim also said he would instruct officials to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders, seven of whom are sheltering in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.
The leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics welcomed Kim's compromises, and confessed he was taken aback by the retreat.

"Today's meeting was not a total solution but there was some advance and President Kim Young-sam showed an attitude of wanting to solve the problems together with opposition parties," Kim Dae-jung told a news conference.
The labour law makes it easier for firms to sack workers and replace strikers. It also bans the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions until 2000.

Kim Dae-jung said that during a lunch meeting at the presidential Blue House he had complained the security law would intimidate intellectuals, journalists, farmers, workers and opposition politicians.
The president had replied "then revise the national security law too", according to Kim Dae-jung, who added "I was very surprised at this".
Both laws were rammed through parliament in a six-minute dawn session on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
Kim Young-sam clipped the wings of the spy agency after he took office in 1993. The new law restores its powers of investigation that were turned over to prosecutors and police.
The security law is chiefly aimed at combatting subversion from communist North Korea.
Kim Young-sam said the labour legislation was intended to revitalise the economy, but instead it had created problems by triggering wildcat strikes that had caused huge losses.
Latest figures show production losses from the stoppages would cost the country more than $3 billion. Export losses were put at $483 million.
The presidential spokesman said Kim rejected opposition demands that both laws be scrapped, saying it would be unconstitutional.
Also present at the meeting were Kim Jong-pil, leader of the small United Liberal Democratic Party and Lee Hong-koo, chairman of the ruling New Korea Party.

President Kim agreed to the meeting on Monday in a dramatic about-face. He had previously insisted the laws could neither be revised nor scrapped and he rejected repeated demands by opposition leaders for dialogue.
The spokesman quoted the president as saying the laws "had made the situation in our economy more difficult, causing public anxiety".
"The purpose of politics is to make people comfortable," Kim was quoted as saying.
